title: Two Villages, One Helicopter
scenario: After a monsoon landslide cuts every road in northern Nepal's Rasuwa district, district coordinator Pema Sherpa has a single helicopter with fuel for one more round trip before dark. Village A, reachable in ten minutes, has eleven injured people, two of them critical. Village B, forty minutes away, reports about sixty people stranded on a failing slope with no known injuries but rising water beneath them. Radio contact with B is intermittent, and its figures are unverified. Pema must decide where the aircraft goes.
options: Send the helicopter to Village A, where the injuries are confirmed and the critically hurt people can be treated within the hour.
Send it to Village B, because the larger group faces a possible collapse and cannot be reached by any other means tonight.
Split the trip, carrying the two critical patients from A first and then attempting a shortened, riskier run toward B if fuel allows.
tension: certain harm vs. uncertain larger harm

title: The Last Insulin in the Shelter
scenario: A cyclone has flooded the coastal town of Pemba in Mozambique, and nurse supervisor Amélia Cossa runs a school-turned-shelter for 400 people. The cooler holds enough insulin for the nine known diabetic residents for two days, but resupply is at least four days away. Two more people arrive that evening, a child newly diagnosed and an elderly man who did not bring his medication. Sharing everything means every patient is under-dosed. Amélia must decide how to ration.
options: Give every diabetic patient a reduced but equal dose so that nobody is cut off entirely, accepting higher risk for all.
Give full doses to those with the best chance of surviving the four days, and give the least stable patients minimal care.
Keep a small reserve unused for emergencies such as ketoacidosis, and divide the rest equally among current patients.

title: Rescue Before the Aftershock Window
scenario: In a collapsed apartment block in Gaziantep, search team leader Mehmet Aydın hears tapping from two separate voids. One, under a staircase, probably holds a pregnant woman who can be reached in about two hours. The other, deeper, may hold three people, including a child, but needs shoring and heavy cutting that could take eight hours. A seismologist warns that a strong aftershock may arrive within six hours, and workers digging near unstable concrete would be at real risk. Mehmet has only one crew. He must choose how to commit them.
options: Commit the whole crew to the staircase void, where a rescue is likely and the risk to rescuers is lower.
Commit the crew to the deeper void, since more lives, including a child's, may depend on it despite the lower odds.
Pull the crew off both for safety checks first, accepting delay to reduce the chance of losing rescuers.

title: Whose Warehouse Gets the Generator
scenario: A winter ice storm has knocked out power across rural Manitoba for days. Emergency manager Dawn Whitecloud controls one portable generator. A seniors' care home on one side of town has backup power failing within hours. On the other side, a community cooperative warehouse holds frozen food and vaccines for three First Nations communities, worth months of supplies, which will spoil without refrigeration by morning. Moving the generator later is impractical. Dawn must decide where it goes tonight.
options: Deploy the generator to the care home, protecting residents who are immediately vulnerable to cold and equipment failure.
Deploy it to the warehouse, protecting the supplies that many remote households will depend on for weeks.
Ask the care home to evacuate residents to the school gymnasium, and send the generator to the warehouse.
tension: immediate vulnerability vs. wider future need
care for individuals vs. community welfare

title: Triage Tags at the Stadium
scenario: After a bridge collapse in Medellín, Dr. Valentina Ríos is the senior physician at a stadium triage point receiving over a hundred casualties with limited surgeons. A man in his sixties arrives with a severe head injury and low odds. A teenager has a treatable but time-sensitive abdominal bleed. A paramedic quietly says the man is the city's deputy mayor, and officials are pressuring staff to prioritize him. Valentina holds the tags and must decide who goes to the one available operating room first.
options: Prioritize the teenager for surgery, since the survival odds are better and the deputy mayor's status should carry no weight.
Prioritize the deputy mayor, arguing that his continued role could help coordinate the whole city's recovery.
Run the two operations sequentially by clinical timing alone, and tell officials only that the tags follow standard protocol.

title: Evacuate the Dam Town or Wait
scenario: A crack has appeared in an earthen dam above the Tamil Nadu town of Kadambur after record rains. Engineer Lakshmi Venkatesan estimates a thirty percent chance of failure within twelve hours. Collector Sundar Raj must decide about ordering evacuation of 9,000 people, which would send frail patients, pregnant women and livestock-dependent farmers onto crowded roads in the dark. Previous false alarms have made residents distrust official orders. If the dam holds, the evacuation might cause injuries and lost livelihoods for nothing. Sundar must decide now.
options: Order a full immediate evacuation, accepting the harms of a possibly unnecessary movement to avoid a catastrophic flood.
Order evacuation only for low-lying wards closest to the dam, and prepare the rest to move quickly if conditions worsen.
Hold off on evacuation while engineers attempt emergency reinforcement for several hours, with transport ready to deploy.
tension: precaution vs. certain harms of acting

title: Sandbags for the Rich Street or the Poor
scenario: As the Rhine approaches record levels near a small German town, volunteer fire chief Katrin Oswald has enough sandbags to protect either the old riverside street of art galleries and expensive homes or the lower district of prefabricated flats, home to many migrants and pensioners. The galleries street is better insured and has more recoverable value to rebuild. The flats have fewer resources to recover from a loss. Both sections will be breached if the surge reaches the forecast peak. Katrin must decide where to build the barrier.
options: Protect the flats district, because its residents have the least capacity to absorb a flood loss.
Protect the galleries street, because the barrier is shorter there and likely to hold, saving more total property.
Build a combined shorter barrier that protects the highest-risk buildings in both districts, leaving some in each exposed.

title: The Field Hospital's Only Ventilator
scenario: During a cholera and measles outbreak after floods in South Sudan's Jonglei state, clinic lead Dr. Achol Deng has one working oxygen concentrator and one mobile ventilator. A seven-year-old with severe measles pneumonia needs it. So does a mother of four with respiratory failure from another cause, and the clinic's best nurse, who contracted the illness while caring for patients. Evacuation to a bigger hospital is impossible for at least a day. Achol must decide how the equipment will be used over the next critical hours.
options: Give the ventilator to the child, whose life ahead is longest and whose illness is most responsive to short-term support.
Give it to the nurse, since her survival would let her go on treating dozens of people in the outbreak.
Allocate by a strict clinical score, setting aside age, role and family, and reassess every few hours.

title: Reopening the Road to Looters and Farmers
scenario: In the Philippines, a typhoon has left the town of Balete cut off from supply convoys. Municipal councilor Ramon Dizon learns that a narrow mountain track could carry food trucks but passes through land owned by a family who refuse access, fearing theft and damage to their terraced crops. A bulldozer could clear a path by force within the hour, using emergency powers that legally permit it. Residents are rationing the last rice. Ramon must decide whether to override the family's refusal.
options: Use emergency powers and clear the track now, compensating the family afterward, so food reaches the town without delay.
Spend a few more hours negotiating with the family, offering payment and guards, before using any force.
Airlift only the most urgent supplies by small boat and aircraft, leaving the family's land untouched, even if less food arrives.

title: Burn the Fireline Through a Vineyard
scenario: Incident commander Hugo Marais faces a wildfire moving toward the Western Cape town of Franschhoek. His crew can create a backburn that would protect the town's 3,000 homes but will destroy a family vineyard and the farmworkers' cottages on it, where eleven families live, many without legal residency papers. The farmworkers could be evacuated, but only if they trust and respond to a warning, which has been unreliable in earlier incidents. Winds are shifting, leaving about forty minutes. Hugo must decide whether to light the backburn.
options: Light the backburn after a final evacuation warning, protecting the larger town while accepting the loss of the vineyard.
Delay the backburn until door-to-door checks confirm the cottages are empty, even if the town's margin of safety shrinks.
Use available aircraft to drop retardant on the town's edge instead, avoiding the backburn but risking a wider breach.
tension: greater good vs. harm to a few

title: Food Aid Lines and the Quiet Village
scenario: Aid logistics officer Ingrid Solheim is deployed after a drought-driven famine alert in the Somali region of Ethiopia. She has enough grain for 6,000 people. The main camp holds 4,500 visible, registered displaced people who press loudly for rations. A nomadic settlement two days away, around 3,000 people with no phone signal and few representatives, probably faces comparable need but cannot be verified. Delivery there would burn extra fuel and delay supplies to the camp. Ingrid must decide how to divide the grain.
options: Distribute everything at the main camp, where need is verified and distribution is manageable and accountable.
Send roughly half toward the remote settlement, trusting reports of need though the numbers cannot be confirmed.
Distribute at the camp now and send a scouting team to assess the settlement, delaying any commitment there.

title: Shelter Beds and the Unregistered Guests
scenario: Following an earthquake in Naples, school principal and shelter coordinator Giulia Fanelli has 220 cots in the gymnasium and 340 people waiting. The civil protection office has instructed her to admit only residents with documentation of a local address. Dozens of those queuing are tourists, seasonal fruit pickers and undocumented residents whose papers were lost with their homes. Temperatures will drop near freezing. Giulia must decide whether to follow the registration rule or admit people by arrival and need.
options: Follow the rule strictly, so beds go to documented residents, which keeps the shelter orderly and avoids official sanction.
Admit people first-come, first-served regardless of papers, accepting the consequences from the civil protection office.
Admit by vulnerability, prioritizing children, elderly and sick people among all groups, and turn away the healthiest adults.

title: Radio Silence on the Missing Trawler
scenario: Coast guard duty officer Tomasz Kruk in Gdynia receives two simultaneous distress calls during a Baltic gale. A fishing trawler reports four crew in the water after capsizing, about fifty minutes away. A ferry reports engine failure and drifting toward a breakwater with 180 passengers, roughly thirty minutes away, though its captain says he may be able to anchor. Only one rescue vessel is within reach, and the other must come from further away. Tomasz must decide where the nearer vessel goes first.
options: Send the vessel to the trawler crew, since people already in cold water have only minutes of survivable time.
Send it to the ferry, since a grounding could endanger many more lives and the vessel can help stabilize it.
Send the vessel toward the trawler but redirect the helicopter to the ferry, accepting that neither response will be complete.

title: Flood Sirens in a Language Few Understand
scenario: Emergency communications chief Aroha Tipene in Gisborne, New Zealand, must send an urgent evacuation alert as a river rises. Her system can broadcast one clear, short message in the next five minutes, or a longer multilingual one in about twenty. Many residents in the affected low-lying area speak Samoan, Tongan or te reo Māori as a first language, and some older people may not parse the English text. Delay could cost lives on roads already filling with water. Aroha must decide how the first alert goes out.
options: Send the short English alert immediately to start movement, then follow with translations as they are finished.
Wait for the multilingual alert so that everyone receives comprehensible instructions at the same time.
Send a short alert in English with simple pictograms and the three most common languages, accepting some imperfect wording.

title: Morgue Space and Family Wishes
scenario: After a heatwave-linked power failure in a Seville retirement district, forensic coordinator Dr. Javier Montoya faces more than ninety bodies in temporary storage and refrigeration that is failing. Many families want to see their relatives and arrange traditional burial within a day, as their faith requires. Official protocol calls for formal identification and autopsy review, which will take about a week and risk decomposition. Javier has authority to release bodies after photographic identification. He must decide how fast to proceed.
options: Release bodies quickly after photographic identification, respecting religious practice and avoiding deterioration in storage.
Insist on the full protocol before any release, preserving evidence about failures that may have caused the deaths.
Release those families who request it with documentation and samples taken, and put the rest through full protocol.

title: Boats at the Lake That Floods Both Banks
scenario: A glacial lake outburst threatens the Peruvian valley below Huaraz. Local civil defense head Rosario Quispe has twelve rescue boats. The downstream town has a modern hospital and about 5,000 residents; upstream hamlets, roughly 600 people mostly Quechua-speaking farmers, would be hit first with less warning. Moving the boats upstream leaves the town thinly covered if the flood is larger than modeled. Moving them downstream means upstream residents must rely on walking to high ground. Rosario must allocate the fleet within the hour.
options: Position most boats downstream, where the numbers and critical infrastructure are greatest, and let the hamlets use evacuation paths.
Position most boats upstream, because those residents will be hit first and have the least capacity to escape alone.
Divide the fleet roughly in proportion to the estimated time-to-impact and mobility of residents in each area.

title: A Drone Feed Nobody Is Supposed to Use
scenario: Rescue coordinator Kenji Morimoto in Ishikawa, Japan, is directing the response to a major earthquake when a hobbyist shares drone footage showing a person waving from a collapsed warehouse. The footage was taken in a no-fly zone set up to protect military helicopters, and the hobbyist could be prosecuted. Using it would send a team to a verified survivor but divert them from a school area where other searches are underway. Kenji must decide whether to act on the unauthorised footage, and how.
options: Use the footage and send a team now, then handle the legal question about the no-fly zone afterwards.
Decline the footage as a matter of principle to preserve the integrity of airspace rules, and keep to the existing plan.
Use the information but quietly protect the hobbyist's identity and ask the airspace authority for a rapid, formal exception.
tension: rule integrity vs. saving a life

title: Fuel for the Clinic or the Bus Convoy
scenario: After a hurricane in Haiti's Grand'Anse, logistics volunteer Jean-Baptiste Pierre holds the last 400 liters of diesel in a region where fuel is unavailable. A rural clinic's generator needs about 300 liters to keep running a week, including a small maternity ward and vaccine fridge. A church group wants it for buses to evacuate 200 people from a village at risk of a second landslide. There is not enough for both. Jean-Baptiste, who has custody and no formal authority, must decide who gets the fuel.
options: Give the fuel to the clinic, protecting ongoing medical care and vaccines for hundreds of people in the area.
Give the fuel to the evacuation buses, moving 200 people away from a plausible landslide before heavy rain returns.
Give the buses just enough for a one-way evacuation and the clinic the remainder, running at reduced hours.
tension: ongoing care vs. preventing a possible disaster

title: Priority List Written in Advance
scenario: Municipal health director Dr. Ewa Lindqvist in Gothenburg is rewriting the city's pandemic surge triage plan before the next crisis. A citizen panel is divided. Some members want ICU priority for patients most likely to survive; others want a lottery among all eligible patients; still others want frontline workers and caregivers of dependent children moved up. The plan will be public and cannot be revised mid-crisis without confusion. Ewa has to recommend a framework to the city council by Friday.
options: Recommend priority based on likelihood of survival alone, applying the same medical criteria to every patient.
Recommend a lottery among patients who meet a minimum survival threshold, to avoid favoring any social group.
Recommend survival likelihood with additional priority for essential workers and sole caregivers, openly stating the reasoning.

title: Choosing Which Grandmother to Wake
scenario: During a volcanic ash emergency near Goma in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, volunteer Chantal Mbuyi has a motorbike and time for two more trips from the evacuation zone. Three households remain: an elderly couple with a bedridden relative who cannot ride, a young family with an infant but a working truck that is out of fuel, and a lone teacher caring for six orphans from a school. Chantal knows that the roads will close in an hour. She must decide whom to reach first.
options: Take the orphans' teacher first, since six children cannot move themselves and have the fewest alternatives.
Go to the elderly household and organise a stretcher carry, since they are least able to move at all.
Bring fuel to the family's truck so that it can carry others as well, instead of transporting anyone herself.

title: The Evacuation Order and the Prison Wing
scenario: A hurricane is approaching the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, and Sheriff's deputy Marcus Tillery, shift commander at a county jail, has been told evacuation transport will not arrive in time for 140 pretrial detainees. Staff can try to move the 40 most medically fragile by van. Alternatively they could release low-level detainees on their own recognisance to find shelter, though some have no homes and one has a protective order against him. Leaving everyone inside risks flooding of the ground floor. Marcus must decide the plan.
options: Evacuate medically fragile detainees by van and shelter the rest in the upper floors, maintaining custody.
Release low-level, non-violent detainees immediately, and keep higher-risk ones in the upper floors with extra staff.
Request an emergency judicial order for mass release, delaying action while the court is contacted despite the closing weather window.
tension: custody duty vs. safety of detainees

title: A Hospital Roof and a Helicopter's Weight
scenario: Flash floods in Zhengzhou have trapped patients on the upper floors of a district hospital with failing power. Air rescue pilot Wei Zhang can land on the roof, but only for about ten minutes and with a weight limit. Waiting there are eight neonatal infants on portable ventilators, six dialysis patients, and a surgeon who says she can stay and keep treating others for the next day. The roof can't take everyone. Wei must decide who flies on this trip.
options: Fly out the neonates with their equipment, since their survival depends most on uninterrupted power and care.
Fly out the dialysis patients, who can stay stable for hours but face serious risk if care is missed for long.
Take the neonates and the surgeon's equipment request, leaving dialysis patients for the next trip.

title: Drinking Water for the Camp or the Cattle
scenario: In northern Kenya's Turkana County, a drought has reduced a borehole to a trickle. Water officer Lokiru Ekai must apportion it among 2,000 people at a relief camp and the herds of nearby pastoralist families, who consider livestock their only wealth and survival insurance. Giving priority to humans means herds could die within days, wiping out families' future livelihoods. Giving water to herds leaves camp members, mostly children, at risk of dehydration. Lokiru must set the allocation today.
options: Allocate all available water to people, and accept that many herds will be lost as a consequence.
Allocate a significant share to the herds, since without livestock families will have no future even if they survive now.
Give people the minimum safe amount and use the remainder for a limited number of breeding animals per family.

title: Blackout Night in a Smart-Ambulance City
scenario: When a cyberattack disables the dispatch software in Tallinn, ambulance coordinator Mari Tamm switches to paper maps and radio. Calls are arriving faster than crews. Two require immediate attention: an elderly man with chest pain at a known address, and a caller who gives a garbled location and may be a child alone with an injured parent. The nearest crew can reach the first in six minutes but the second only after searching the district for perhaps twenty. Mari must decide where to send that crew.
options: Send the crew to the confirmed address with the chest pain, where success is likely and the location is certain.
Send the crew to search for the garbled caller, since a child may be in danger with no one else to help.
Send the crew to the chest pain case and request police patrol cars to search for the unclear caller simultaneously.
tension: limited resources vs. moral weight of a child

title: Cutting a Trapped Man's Leg in the Surf
scenario: On a Samoan reef flat, paramedic volunteer Tui Faleolo reaches a fisherman whose leg is pinned under a boulder displaced by a tsunami surge. The tide is rising and another wave set is forecast in twenty minutes. A rescue crew with hydraulic tools needs about forty minutes to arrive. Tui has a saw and training, but no anaesthetic beyond a small dose of analgesic, and the man is conscious and begging her not to cut. She must decide what to do in the time remaining.
options: Attempt amputation to free him before the next waves, accepting the severe harm to save his life.
Stay with him and try to hold his head above water and shield him, honoring his refusal and waiting for the crew.
Try levering the boulder with available tools for ten minutes first, deciding on amputation only if conditions deteriorate.
tension: irreversible harm vs. risk of death
